Orient layers so centrifugal/bending loads run in-plane, not across layers. Below Re~60k use a thin high-camber sharp-LE section, not a scaled Clark-Y. Verify printed twist with calipers.

vtol_levers.name: Unidirectional carbon spar/boom, printed parts only as shear web and connectors
vtol_levers.mechanism: FDM polymers have low specific stiffness (PLA E~3.5 GPa) and weak interlayer bonds, so a fully-printed spar is heavy for its bending stiffness and delaminates. Bending stiffness E*I wants material far from the neutral axis, so put it in pultruded carbon caps/tubes (E~120-150 GPa) and let the print be only the low-stress shear web, ribs, and locating sockets.
vtol_levers.impact: WEIGHT FRACTION + all phases. A carbon-capped spar is typically 40-60% lighter than an equivalent all-printed box spar at equal tip deflection, and stiffer wings hold the cruise airfoil shape (less washout/flutter) so effective L/D holds up. Also stiffens the two tilt booms, cutting vibration-driven control loss in hover and transition.
vtol_levers.cost: Weight negative (saves). Money low-moderate ($5-15/airframe of carbon). Complexity medium: needs accurate bonded sockets and interference/epoxy fit, adds a bonding step and a non-printed BOM item.
vtol_levers.printable_implementation: Design the wing as printed rib-and-shear-web sections threaded onto a pultruded carbon tube (~8-10 mm OD) with printed collar sockets at +0.1-0.15 mm slip+epoxy clearance. Route two carbon booms wing-to-nacelle the same way. Split the wing into 2-3 spanwise print segments keyed on the spar to fit the bed.

vtol_levers.name: Flight scheduling: rush the transition corridor and cruise at best-L/D / min-power speed
vtol_levers.mechanism: Hover power is ~7x cruise for this class (~443 W vs ~60 W), so time in hover and the stalled transition window is the dominant discretionary drain. The wing makes no useful lift below ~1.2*Vstall (~12-14 m/s), so driving forward acceleration hard during tilt unloads the rotors and collapses power toward cruise sooner. Separately, cruise power = drag*V with parasitic (~V^2) and induced (~1/V^2) terms giving a min-power/best-L/D speed; the baseline cruises at CL~0.42, above L/D-max on the parasitic side, so trimming a few m/s slower recovers L/D. (Merges the hover-dwell, airspeed-schedule, and wing-loading/cruise-CL-trim candidates.)
vtol_levers.impact: RANGE + TRANSITION, entirely free of hardware. Cruising toward best-L/D can add ~10-20% range; correct transition airspeed avoids the power spike and shaves seconds of high-power operation per cycle (each 10 s ~0.8% of a 150 Wh pack). On multi-hop missions the cumulative saving is 5-15% of usable energy. Lower transition speed also narrows the stall/transition gap, a safety positive.
vtol_levers.cost: Essentially free: control-law/tuning plus careful flight testing to find real best-L/D and safe transition airspeed. Needs a decent FC (e.g. ArduPlane QuadPlane) with tuned transition-airspeed and tilt-rate params and clean airspeed sensing. Small structural-load penalty from higher transition acceleration. Trades trip time for energy.
vtol_levers.printable_implementation: No aero surface change. Print a vibration-isolated pitot mount ahead of the prop wash and out of the fuselage boundary layer for trustworthy airspeed. Print low-backlash tilt gearing (herringbone/preloaded, captive-nut hard points) so commanded tilt rate is achieved. Add a trim-adjustable elevator/servo tab so cruise trim dials to best-L/D without re-slicing. Log via the FC and iterate. Use conservative CLmax (~1.0-1.1) at Re 150-300k when setting transition airspeed.

vtol_levers.name: Print orientation aligned to the principal load path
vtol_levers.mechanism: FDM is strongly anisotropic: interlayer (Z) tensile strength is only ~30-60% of in-plane. Tilt booms, motor arms and the tilt yoke see bending that puts a face in tension across layer lines if printed in the wrong pose. Orienting so the primary tensile bead runs along the load lets thinner walls hit the same strength (less mass) and removes the sudden delamination failure mode.
vtol_levers.impact: WEIGHT FRACTION + transition/safety. Correct orientation typically lets you drop 1-2 perimeters (10-25% wall mass) on booms/arms at equal strength, and removes the dominant crash mode in the high-load transition phase where rotor thrust vector and wing lift both load the booms.
vtol_levers.cost: Weight negative-to-neutral, money none, complexity low-medium: some parts need supports or a split+bond to reach the good orientation; requires per-part thinking rather than print-it-flat.
vtol_levers.printable_implementation: Print tilt booms and motor arms with beads running along the boom axis (two-piece bonded tube if longer than the bed), not layers stacked across the axis. Print the tilt yoke so pivot-load beads run continuous around the bearing. Where a part must cross layers in tension, add a carbon pin or filament wrap. Validate with a 3-point bend on a coupon.

vtol_levers.name: Match motor Kv and cell count so hover thrust lands at 50-65% throttle
vtol_levers.mechanism: A BLDC motor + ESC peaks in a mid-load band (~50-70% throttle); below ~30% ESC switching and current-per-thrust losses dominate, near 100% copper (I^2R) losses spike. Kv sets RPM (~Kv*V), so choose prop+Kv+cell-count so static thrust equals weight at ~55% throttle. Over-Kv'd motors force tiny inefficient twitchy openings in hover; under-Kv'd motors bog and overheat.
vtol_levers.impact: HOVER + TRANSITION, plus range indirectly. Moving the hover point from ~35% to ~55% throttle typically recovers 5-15% of drivetrain electrical efficiency (motor+ESC eta ~70% toward ~82-85%) and improves control authority and thermal margin during the transition surge.
vtol_levers.cost: Essentially free if chosen at design time (right motor SKU + cell count); expensive to fix later (re-motor/re-cell). Needs a thrust-stand measurement or a good manufacturer thrust table plus an AUW estimate.
vtol_levers.printable_implementation: Design motor mounts with a parametric bolt circle (16/19/25 mm) and a swappable printed motor-boss insert so a different Kv/frame-size drops in without reprinting the nacelle. Add printed cooling scoops/vents over ESC and motor (transition is the thermal worst case). Print a bolt-on thrust-stand cradle to measure the real thrust-vs-throttle curve before committing.

vtol_levers.name: Higher aspect ratio wing (span extension / tapered planform)
vtol_levers.mechanism: Induced drag CDi = CL^2/(pi*e*AR). At baseline AR~7.3, CL~0.42, raising AR to 10-12 (longer span at same area, or reduced chord) cuts CDi materially. Because a tiltrotor carries the wing as dead weight in hover there is a real optimum: too much span raises structural mass and hover bending, but in the induced-drag-limited part of the polar the gain is direct, and it grows once CD0 is reduced.
vtol_levers.impact: CRUISE + RANGE. L/D rises from ~9.4 toward ~10.3 at AR 12 in the current CD0-dominated budget; payoff grows to +10-15% L/D once CD0 drops and induced drag becomes a bigger share. Slightly HURTS hover (more spanwise mass/inertia, longer roll arm, heavier wing). Transition mildly positive (cleaner wing-borne lift onset).
vtol_levers.cost: Medium: longer span needs a stiffer/heavier spar to survive cruise gusts and hover download; weight penalty scales more than linearly with span. Multi-section printing/joining adds complexity. Pairs naturally with the carbon-spar lever.
vtol_levers.printable_implementation: Print the wing in spanwise segments over a continuous carbon tube bonded through printed ribs; keep skin a thin shell (1.2-2 mm, 2-3 perimeters) with sparse gyroid only near root. Add printed spar caps or an embedded carbon strip for bending stiffness without solid infill. Taper the planform (tip chord ~0.6 root) to approximate elliptic loading and push e toward ~0.9.

vtol_levers.name: Surface finish + low-Re laminar-flow airfoil on the wing
vtol_levers.mechanism: At cruise the wing runs Re ~150k-350k where CD0 (skin-friction + pressure drag) is ~3-4x induced drag at CL~0.42. FDM layer lines (0.1-0.2 mm ridges) act as distributed roughness that trips the boundary layer early and can spawn a laminar separation bubble that spikes profile drag. Sealing/smoothing plus a section designed for this Re band (SD7037, E387, S9000-class) keeps flow attached and shrinks the bubble, cutting profile drag ~15-30%.
vtol_levers.impact: CRUISE + RANGE: dropping CD0 from ~0.035 to ~0.028 lifts L/D from ~9.4 to ~11 at the same CL, a ~15-20% range/endurance gain. Modest hover benefit (lower cruise power frees battery for hover reserve). Neutral on transition.
vtol_levers.cost: Low money, low weight. Cost is labor: filler-primer, wet-sand to ~400-600 grit, optionally a thin heat-shrink/glass skin (~30-80 g on a 1.6 m wing). Airfoil swap is free at design time, costly to retrofit.
vtol_levers.printable_implementation: Print with span axis vertical or use ironing on top surfaces to minimize layer-line roughness in the flow direction; keep seams off the LE suction peak. Model as a thin shell, prime + wet-sand the leading 40% of chord. Add a trip strip at 30-40% chord ONLY if flight data shows a persistent bubble. Use a validated low-Re coordinate set, not a scaled full-size section.

vtol_levers.name: Battery chemistry, voltage, and capacity matched to the phase power profile
vtol_levers.mechanism: Range scales with usable Wh/kg. LiPo gives high C for the brief hover/transition surge but ~180-200 Wh/kg; 21700 high-drain Li-ion gives ~250-280 Wh/kg with limited continuous C. A tiltrotor spends seconds at high power and minutes-hours cruising, so a Li-ion or Li-ion-dominant pack is often range-optimal, sized so hover surge current (I=P_hover/V) stays inside the C rating. Higher pack voltage lowers current for the same power, cutting I^2R losses in wiring/connectors/ESC and allowing thinner lighter wire. Do not oversize: dead battery mass costs range roughly linearly.
vtol_levers.impact: RANGE dominant (usable range can swing 20-40% via Wh/kg alone), plus a few percent system efficiency from higher voltage. Wrong chemistry either can't supply hover current (need LiPo) or wastes range (LiPo where Li-ion would do). Touches hover, transition, cruise and range together.
vtol_levers.cost: Money (high-drain Li-ion and higher-voltage ESCs cost more) and packaging; higher voltage needs matching motor/ESC ratings; under-sized Li-ion risks sag during the hover surge.
vtol_levers.printable_implementation: Print a sliding battery tray with detents to trim CG in flight test (hover-vs-cruise CG shift is a real tiltrotor issue). Print vented 21700 holders with a snug non-compressive fit if going Li-ion. Recess an XT60/XT90 with strain relief and route short fat power leads straight to the ESCs to minimize resistance.

vtol_levers.name: Smooth blade surfaces and sharpen LE/TE (recover print-vs-molded prop loss)
vtol_levers.mechanism: At blade Re<~150k the boundary layer is largely laminar and separation-prone; FDM layer lines act as large relative roughness that trips and thickens it, raising section Cd and cutting thrust, and a blunt printed TE (nozzle-limited ~0.4 mm) adds base drag and noise. Low-Re prop studies show a smoothed 3D-printed rotor can match a commercial rotor's aero and acoustics. This is the concrete execution of the Reynolds-aware prop guardrail: pick diameter/RPM for the highest practical blade Re at Mtip<~0.4, then finish the blade.
vtol_levers.impact: HOVER: +3-6% thrust/power recovery (a couple points of FoM), more on a rough print. Equal benefit to CRUISE prop efficiency and lower noise. Net positive across ALL phases; it is pure loss-recovery, and it also serves as a guardrail against over-estimating thrust/endurance from paper (high-Re) prop efficiencies.
vtol_levers.cost: Labor, not weight or money: sanding/vapor-smoothing time. Small risk of altering the airfoil if over-sanded. Vapor smoothing needs ABS/ASA (acetone) rather than PETG/PLA. Guardrail portion is free analysis discipline.
vtol_levers.printable_implementation: Print aero surfaces at <=0.12 mm layers with lines running spanwise, wet-sand 400->800 grit, finish with filler-primer (acetone-vapor for ABS/ASA). Hand-thin the TE to <0.5 mm and round the LE to the design radius. Prefer bought carbon/nylon props for the primary discs and print only the hub adapter; if printing, balance every prop. Payoff is largest on the smallest/slowest-tip rotors.

vtol_levers.name: Thin-wall aft structure, tips, and fairings as sacrificial low-inertia mass
vtol_levers.mechanism: Aft of the spar the structure carries little bending load, but naive prints put 2-3 solid perimeters everywhere, adding mass far from CG and at the tips where it inflates roll/yaw inertia. At cruise chord Re~2.7e5 the airfoil is forgiving, so surfaces aft of the spar only need to hold shape, not carry load: make them single-perimeter skin over sparse ribs or a printed lattice.
vtol_levers.impact: WEIGHT FRACTION + hover/transition control. Typically 40-100 g off the wing, concentrated at tips/TE so it cuts roll and yaw inertia disproportionately for snappier, less power-hungry attitude control in hover and cleaner transition.
vtol_levers.cost: Weight negative, money none, complexity low. Trade: thin skins are fragile to handling, accepted as sacrificial/repairable. Below chord Re~1e5 (tiny tips) keep skins smooth and avoid ultra-rough sparse lattices so laminar separation doesn't dominate.
vtol_levers.printable_implementation: Slice everything aft of the spar and the outboard tips as 1-perimeter LW-PLA over ribs at ~30-40 mm pitch, or a printed lattice under a 0.5-0.6 mm skin. Keep the LE (impact + laminar-flow-critical) at 2 smooth perimeters. Make the tip a removable/replaceable printed part so crash damage is a cheap reprint. Consolidating each nacelle into fewer monolithic prints with press-fit bearing seats is a related nearly-free 60-160 g win in the same spirit.

issues: [cg_ballast] CRITICAL PHYSICS ERROR: The concept computes static margin as the offset between CG and the WING aerodynamic centre (0.25 MAC). That is only valid for a tailless flying wing. Keelhaul has a V-tail on an aft boom, so the aircraft NEUTRAL POINT sits well aft of the wing AC (the tail adds pitch stiffness). Correct static margin = (NP - CG)/MAC, not (AC - CG)/MAC. The headline claim 'CG-to-AC offset alone sets the static margin / gives +10%' is methodologically wrong. Corrected wording throughout to distinguish NP from AC and to credit the tail.

[cg_ballast] GEOMETRY vs CLAIM CONTRADICTION: Concept states the 0.25-MAC AC 'lands at y~47', but its own diagram wing root runs LE y=38 to TE y=52 (chord 14 units), so 0.25c is at y=41.5, not 47. The stated CG y=45 is therefore actually ~3.5 units (25% chord) BEHIND the true wing AC, i.e. tail-heavy relative to the wing alone. The plane is only stable because of the tail it argued away. Fixed: cg_point moved to y=41 (just ahead of wing AC y=41.5); corrected all AC/CG numbers to match the diagram.

[cg_ballast] PRINTABILITY IMPOSSIBILITY: 'print-in-place TPU living hinge printed flat as part of the (LW-PLA/PETG) surface' cannot be done on a single-nozzle printer — you cannot embed a TPU web inside a PLA/PETG part in one pass. Corrected to either an integral thin-web PLA/PETG print-in-place hinge (works, but fatigues) or an explicit multi-material printer requirement; build_difficulty raised to 'hard' to reflect the multi-material/carbon/foaming-PLA process stack.

[cg_ballast] EFFICIENCY OVERCLAIM (mass): 'saves 30-80 g of dead lead vs tail-heavy beginner builds' benchmarks against a strawman bad design. Deliberate component placement for CG is standard practice, not a novel efficiency gain. Reframed as good practice, not a quantified 5-8% endurance win.

[cg_ballast] EFFICIENCY DOUBLE-COUNT: gains (1) mass and (2) trim-drag are presented as 'compounding' but both derive from the same correct-CG decision; the trim-drag figure (3-6% cruise power) is at the optimistic end and only accrues vs a mistrimmed baseline. Softened and de-duplicated.

[cg_ballast] WEIGHT OPTIMISM: 950 g AUW with a 230 g LiPo leaves ~478 g for all printed structure; a realistic LW-PLA airframe (skin+ribs+D-box+bulkheads) for a 1.05 m span is ~400 g, so 950 g is achievable but tight. Corrected AUW to a 950-1050 g band and adjusted the ballast-fraction claim accordingly (~22-24%).
[cg_ballast] MINOR: reynolds_note Re value stated 197,000; recompute V*MAC/nu = 16*0.18/1.5e-5 = 192,000. Trivial, corrected to ~192k.

[high_ar_wing] FATAL: Battery spec is physically impossible. A 500 g 6S LiPo cannot hold 178 Wh (that is 356 Wh/kg, ~2x the best real LiPo at 150-180 Wh/kg). A real 500 g pack holds ~85-90 Wh. You can honor at most two of {500 g, 178 Wh, 1.8 kg AUW}. Corrected to a real ~90 Wh / 500 g pack, keeping AUW 1.8 kg.

[high_ar_wing] RANGE OVERCLAIM: 200-230 km depends entirely on the impossible 178 Wh figure. With a real 90 Wh pack at AUW 1.8 kg and honest drag, cruise range is ~110-140 km, not 200+. Corrected to ~120 km (best-case ~140 km at CD0=0.03).

[high_ar_wing] STABILITY REASONING ERROR: The concept uses the WING quarter-chord AC (y=41.5) as the stability reference. The aircraft NEUTRAL POINT sits AFT of the wing AC because the tail contributes lift-curve slope at a moment arm. True static margin is measured against the NP, so the real margin is LARGER (more stable) than the ~8-15% claimed. CG=39.8 ahead of wing-AC=41.5 is still correct and safe; only the reasoning/label is wrong. Corrected wording distinguishes AC from NP.

[high_ar_wing] CRUISE POWER OPTIMISTIC: 30 W assumes a clean CD0~0.03. A quadplane with FOUR exposed lift motors, booms and saddle clamps in the freestream realistically runs CD0~0.04-0.05, cutting cruise L/D to ~11-13 and raising cruise power to ~30-34 W. 30 W is a best-case floor, not nominal. Corrected to ~30-34 W and L/D ~13-14.6 (best case).

[high_ar_wing] HOVER POWER SLIGHTLY OPTIMISTIC: Momentum theory for 4x 10-inch disks lifting 1.8 kg with figure-of-merit 0.65 and motor/ESC eff 0.82 gives ~198 W electrical, not 180 W. Corrected to ~195-200 W (and hover endurance on a real 90 Wh pack ~4-5 min budgeted, but the profile should still be hover-brief).

[high_ar_wing] ROLL-AUTHORITY ARITHMETIC INCONSISTENT: With 270 g thrust headroom per rotor over a 0.45 m arm and two rotors per side, differential roll moment is ~4.8 Nm and ~1140 deg/s^2 (Ixx~0.24), i.e. DOUBLE the quoted 2.4 Nm / 560 deg/s^2. The quoted figures appear to use one rotor per side. The qualitative point (roll is the weak axis due to span^2 inertia) is correct; the numbers were garbled. Corrected to internally consistent values.

[high_ar_wing] MINOR GEOMETRY/HOVER COUPLING: The lift-rotor pair-midpoint in the top view is at y=(33+57)/2=45, which is BEHIND both the AC (41.5) and CG (39.8), not coincident with CG as claimed. This introduces a small hover pitch bias the pusher/attitude loop must trim. Corrected by moving the rear rotor pair forward (y=53) so the pair-midpoint lands at y=43, much closer to CG.

[high_ar_wing] TERMINOLOGY: 'more than halves the induced-drag coefficient' (0.027 -> 0.011 going AR5->AR12) is correct and verified; retained. L/D 14.6 at CL0.6 and LDmax 16.3 verified as arithmetically sound with e=0.85, CD0=0.03; retained as best-case.

[ducted_boxwing] DISK LOADING WRONG BY ~3.4x: two 6-inch (152mm) rotors carrying 1150g give ~310 N/m^2, not the claimed 90 N/m^2. To hit 90 N/m^2 you would need ~11-inch rotors. Corrected to ~310 N/m^2 and flagged as high (power-hungry).

[ducted_boxwing] CRUISE L/D GAIN OVERCLAIMED: 20-30% requires induced drag to dominate. For this draggy ducted box-wing (CD0~0.05, cruise CL~0.5) induced drag is a minority of total drag, so realized net L/D gain is ~5-14%, not 20-30%. Realized span efficiency also degrades from ideal 1.47 to ~1.3 after joints/interference. Corrected.

[ducted_boxwing] GEOMETRY - ASYMMETRIC LIFT DUCTS: both lift-duct motors were placed at x=25 (both on the left wing), which would produce an off-center hover thrust line and an uncontrollable rolling moment. They are fore/aft centerline ducts, so moved to x=50.

[ducted_boxwing] GEOMETRY - COMPONENTS OUTSIDE OUTLINE: GPS (42,26) and Elevon servo (70,66) fell outside the top-view outline (point-in-polygon fail). Moved GPS to (48,28) and elevon servo to (68,70), both now inside.

[ducted_boxwing] SPAR INCONSISTENCY: realization text claimed ONE 6mm carbon spar running through BOTH front and rear wing members, but the two elements are separated fore-aft and by the ~164mm vertical h/b=0.2 gap - a single straight spar cannot pass through both. key_specs correctly says 2 spars. Corrected the wording to two spars (one per element).

[ducted_boxwing] WEIGHT OPTIMISTIC (flagged, not fatal): 360g LW-PLA airframe for an 820mm box-wing with three printed ducts, two spars and tip endplates is tight; realistic is ~400-480g, pushing AUW to ~1200-1300g. Battery mass (330g for 4S3300) and motor/ESC mass are realistic. Adjusted the note to state AUW likely creeps up.

[ducted_boxwing] MINOR: cg_point y nudged from 45 to 47 to stay consistent with the corrected (centerline) component layout; CG remains ahead of the neutral point with a healthy ~10% static margin - stability is sound.

[ducted_boxwing] NON-ISSUE CONFIRMED: the Reynolds verdict is honest. The design correctly discards the paper-ring low-Re anti-separation artifact and keeps only Re-independent potential-flow effects (closed-wing induced-drag reduction, momentum-theory duct augmentation). Hover ENDURANCE (4-5 min) is actually conservative, not overclaimed.

[tailless_flywing] STABILITY (load-bearing error): stated neutral point y=38 is not where the aero NP of this planform sits. For a swept delta/flying-wing (LE apex y=2, mean-chord LE ~y=10-14, MAC ~38 body-units) the NP falls near 25-35% MAC aft of the MAC LE, i.e. ~y=24-28. y=38 is essentially the planform AREA CENTROID (computed y=34) pushed further aft - that is where mass balances, not where the aero NP is. Placing NP ~10 units too far aft makes the design LOOK comfortably stable (CG35 ahead of NP38) while masking that it is actually marginal.

[tailless_flywing] STABILITY: diagram cg_point y=35 is not supported by its own component layout. Integrating listed components (battery 300g@y=20, payload 80g@y=24, GPS/FC ~y=27-31, tilt motors 2x60g@y=30, aft lift motor ~55g@y=44, servos) plus ~500g structure at the planform area centroid (y~34) yields a real CG of y~29-30, i.e. FURTHER FORWARD than claimed y=35. To reach y=35 the structure centroid would have to sit at y~46 (implausibly aft).

[tailless_flywing] STABILITY (net consequence): with corrected NP (~y=33, achievable via the quoted moderate sweep + reflex Cm0) and real CG (~y=30), static margin is ~8% MAC - inside the 5-15% target - but that is NOT the picture the concept paints. As written (real CG ~29-30 vs a first-principles NP as low as ~y=25) the margin could be near zero or negative. Workable, but it is a knife-edge tailless wing whose stability depends on sweep/reflex pushing the NP aft, not the ~10% comfortable buffer implied.

[tailless_flywing] STABILITY (arithmetic): even using the concept's own numbers, SM = (NP-CG)/MAC = (38-35)/38 = 7.9% MAC, not the ~10% repeatedly claimed. The %-MAC figure was asserted, not computed.

[tailless_flywing] REYNOLDS verdict mislabeled: 'does-not-scale' is wrong for the design as a whole. The paper flat-plate airfoil genuinely does not scale to Re~183k (a sharp-edged plate is actively bad there), which the note explains correctly - but the borrowed PRINCIPLE (tailless + reflex + forward-CG stability) is Reynolds-independent and transfers cleanly, as the note itself admits. Verdict should be 'partially-scales': the geometry/stability logic scales, the specific airfoil does not.

[tailless_flywing] EFFICIENCY overclaim: 'cruise power drops 20-30% vs an equivalent tailed layout' is inflated. Removing tail+boom cuts ~15-20% of wetted area, but the tail is only a fraction of total drag and induced drag (the dominant component here, CDi~0.014 vs CD0~0.02-0.025) is unchanged. Realistic cruise-power saving vs a well-designed tailed peer is ~10-15%. The plate->reflex airfoil gain (L/D 4-5 -> 12-14) is a win over the PAPER, not over a real tailed RC wing that would also use a proper airfoil - conflating the two double-counts the benefit.

[tailless_flywing] L/D ceiling optimistic: computed L/D at CL=0.49, AR=6.5, e~0.85 is 12.6 (CD0=0.025) to 14.5 (CD0=0.020). The claimed '12-16' top end of 16 ignores the drag of two tilt nacelles and a windmilling/parked aft lift motor+prop sitting in the wing wake. Trim to ~11-14.

[tailless_flywing] MINOR: cruise CL is 0.49 (matches ~0.5, fine). Reflex sections cap CLmax around 0.9, so Vstall ~11.8 m/s and the 15 m/s transition is only 1.27*Vstall - acceptable but not generous; worth stating explicitly rather than implying comfortable margin.

[autorotation_recovery] STABILITY LOGIC ERROR (primary): The concept argues chordwise static margin using the diagram's y-axis (cg y=35 vs AC y=45). But in this top-view, y is the SPANWISE/radial axis (root->tip, range 8..97) and x is the CHORD (range 38..62). Chordwise CG-vs-AC must be shown on the x-axis. As drawn, every component sits at x~49-51, so the diagram encodes essentially ZERO chordwise margin information; the 'CG ahead of AC' claim is unsupported by the geometry. Fixed by offsetting the spar/battery/FC forward in x (toward the leading edge at low x) and the AC/flap aft in x, so CG_x < AC_x with a real ~8-12% margin.

[autorotation_recovery] LAYOUT CONTRADICTION: Text says motor+prop at the far TIP and battery inboard at the ROOT, but the diagram placed motor at y=12, battery at y=40, and the cyclic flap hinge at y=78 -- leaving the spin-axis/root end ambiguous and the radial mass split incoherent. Corrected so y=8 region is the tip (motor) and the root nacelle (battery/FC/servo/GPS) clusters near the opposite, inboard end, with the flap along the blade near the AC.

[autorotation_recovery] CG_POINT MISMATCH: Stated cg_point y=35 does not match the mass-weighted radial centroid of the placed components (~40). Also cg_x was 50 (no chordwise offset). Corrected to cg_point that reflects both a sane inboard radial position and a genuine forward chordwise offset relative to the 25%-chord AC.

[autorotation_recovery] SPAR DOUBLE-COUNT: The realization prose counts the carbon spar inside both the '~35 g blade (shell+spar)' and the '85 g nacelle/spar/structure' lines. Clarified so the spar is counted once (in the blade line) and the structure line is nacelle+shell-bond+hardware only; totals still ~250 g.

[autorotation_recovery] TIP MOTOR MASS OPTIMISTIC: 25 g for a motor+prop that must generate the full ~250 gf of thrust is on the light edge; a realistic 2204/2306-class motor + 5-6 in prop is ~30-40 g. Adjusted the motor allowance up and trimmed structure to keep AUW ~250 g.

[autorotation_recovery] EFFICIENCY FRAMING OPTIMISTIC (not headlined, but flagged): A naive induced+profile power of ~5 W implies unrealistically long (~50 min) hover endurance. Real single-blade Figure of Merit is low (tip losses, no second blade, hub/torque-reaction losses), plus ESC/motor (~60-70%) and once-per-rev cyclic-servo duty. The ~15-30% hover-power advantage over a same-weight quad is directionally correct (it follows sqrt of the ~7.6x lower disk loading) but the absolute power/endurance should be treated as best-case, not typical.

[autorotation_recovery] AUTOROTATION ROBUSTNESS CAVEAT: The momentum/energy balance for autorotation scales fine, but a SINGLE-blade monocopter has poorer autorotative attitude stability and modest stored rotational KE (~2.4 J), so the flare-arrested touchdown is marginal, not comfortable. Kept as a genuine safety feature but stated as marginal rather than guaranteed.

[energy_glide_profile] STABILITY (critical, internally contradictory): The concept claims CG at y=44 is '~8 box-units / ~10% MAC ahead of the AC at y=52'. But the wing occupies y=46 (LE) to y=56 (TE), so MAC is only ~10 box-units. 8 box-units is therefore ~80% MAC, not 10% — an absurd, unflyable static margin (massive trim download, collapsed L/D, sluggish pitch). The arithmetic '8 units = 10% MAC' is simply wrong.

[energy_glide_profile] STABILITY (AC mislocated): The aerodynamic center is the wing quarter-chord ≈ y=48.5 (LE 46 + 0.25*10), not y=52 as claimed (y=52 is ~60% chord, aft of the AC). Using the correct AC and a sane 8-12% static margin, the CG should sit at y≈47.5, not y=44. A component mass-moment sum of the actual layout naturally lands CG near y≈45-47 (the rear boom motors at y=88 pull it aft), so the claimed forward CG of y=44 both contradicts the layout and would be over-stable.

[energy_glide_profile] EFFICIENCY (L/D overclaim): Best whole-aircraft L/D of 11.7 is optimistic. At Re~150k with a bluff PETG VTOL pod, four motor nacelles, two tail booms, and stopped/feathered props hanging in the airstream, realistic parasite+profile Cd0 ≈ 0.035 and e≈0.75 give L/D_max ≈ 10. Hitting 11.7 would require Cd0≈0.028 (near-clean sailplane), not achievable for a multirotor-capable airframe. Corrected to ~10.

[energy_glide_profile] EFFICIENCY (hover endurance self-inconsistent): The spec states 208 W hover and 59 Wh usable, but then claims ~24 min pure-hover endurance. 59 Wh / 208 W = ~17 min. The 24 min figure contradicts the concept's own power number; corrected to ~17 min.

[energy_glide_profile] EFFICIENCY (range knock-on): Range figures rest on L/D 11.7. At the corrected L/D~10, per-cycle glide is ~1.5 km (not 1.75 km) and total climb-glide range is ~21-23 km (not 24 km); the ~1.6x advantage over powered cruise still holds but is slightly overstated.

[energy_glide_profile] WEIGHT (minor): 450 g for a 4S 5000 mAh LiPo is optimistic — typical packs are ~480-560 g. Overall mass budget still sums to ~1.5-1.6 kg, so AUW is realistic, but the battery mass and 380 g total filament are both on the optimistic edge.

[energy_glide_profile] REGEN claim is directionally right but should stay conservative: prop-as-turbine efficiency at these Re is poor and an unfeathered disk usually costs more glide than it returns — kept as a marginal, steep-descent-only option.

[passive_stability] STABILITY (real bug): The diagram places cg_point at y=40, which is exactly on the wing leading edge (root chord runs y=40 LE to y=54 TE). That is 0% MAC = ~25% static margin, NOT the claimed 10%. Excessively nose-heavy: sluggish pitch response and high trim drag. CG must move aft to y=42.1 (15% MAC) to match the concept's own stated 10% static-margin target.

[passive_stability] STABILITY (coordinate error): The text claims '25% MAC falls at y=46.' False. With LE at y=40 and TE at y=54, y=46 is 42.9% MAC. The true 25%-MAC neutral point is at y=43.5. The weighted_components narrative and the diagram disagree with each other and with basic arithmetic.

[passive_stability] EFFICIENCY (overclaim): L/D 15-18 is quoted as if it applies at the 14 m/s cruise. At cruise CL=0.29 the actual L/D is only ~11-13 (induced drag is tiny there; you're flying well below best-glide CL). L/D 15-18 is the BEST-GLIDE value, which occurs at ~9-10 m/s (CL~0.6-0.7). Corrected to cruise L/D ~12, best-glide/loiter L/D ~15-16; 18 is optimistic and requires CD0<=0.02.
[passive_stability] STABILITY (minor): Payload/camera placed at y=39 and called 'right at the CG,' but the corrected CG is y=42.1. Payload should sit at y~42 so payload swaps don't shift balance.

[passive_stability] EFFICIENCY (soft claim, tempered not fatal): The 'avionics power drops 10-20%' control-energy saving is hand-wavy — servo holding current on a small survey plane is a few watts, a minor slice of total (mostly propulsion) power. Reframed as a gust-rejection/latency benefit with a small avionics saving rather than a headline efficiency number.

[passive_stability] CONFIG (contradiction): drone_type says '2-axis elevon OR rudder+elevator' but the diagram shows elevon servos and no horizontal tail. Resolved as a tailless/plank elevon layout (which is what justifies neutral-point ~= wing AC at 25% MAC); optional small vertical fin/rudder for Dutch-roll damping retained.

[snapfit_structure] HOVER ARCHITECTURE BROKEN (critical): the drone is defined as two tilting front nacelles + one FIXED pusher. A fixed pusher's thrust is horizontal and contributes ZERO lift in hover, so hover rests on only the 2 front rotors at y~30 -- both AHEAD of the CG (y~40). Two lift points forward of CG cannot trim pitch; the craft pitches nose-down uncontrollably with no aft lift point. The 'tri-motor VTOL, T/W 1.8' spec also double-counts the horizontal pusher (2 of 3 motors give T/W~1.2, not 1.8). Fixed by making the rear motor a TILTING rotor (true tri-tiltrotor) so it lifts in hover and, sitting aft of CG at y~88, provides pitch authority.

[snapfit_structure] STATIC MARGIN INCOHERENT / OVERSTATED: with no horizontal tail the neutral point ~= wing AC (~y48). The wing chord maps to only ~11 y-units, so CG@40 vs NP@48 = ~73% static margin, NOT the claimed 8-10% -- that is uncontrollably nose-heavy, the opposite of a trimmable cruiser. For a real ~9% SM the CG must sit ~y47. Fixed: CG moved to (50,47); battery/FC/GPS y-stations shifted aft; wording corrected so the aircraft is genuinely near ~8-10% MAC.

[snapfit_structure] EFFICIENCY OVERCLAIM: 'forward CG => 10-20% less cruise current' is unphysical. Static stability lowers pilot workload and gust sensitivity, not cruise power. Trim drag for a sane SM is only ~1-4% of cruise power, and a MORE forward CG INCREASES up-elevator trim drag (the opposite of a saving). Fixed: efficiency gain rewritten to credit the real structural mass savings plus an honest ~1-3% operational effect, removing the 'stability = free energy' framing.

[snapfit_structure] L/D OPTIMISTIC: drag buildup (CDi at AR~4.1, e~0.75, section CD0~0.022, plus fat PETG pod + two tilt nacelles + exposed carbon spar + snap-fit seam steps ~0.020) gives cruise L/D ~7.6, ~8.9 best-case -- not 9-11. Fixed: L/D revised to ~7-9 in principle, specs, and efficiency sections.

[snapfit_structure] MINOR: hover figure of merit and disk loading were never stated; added momentum-theory hover numbers. GEOMETRY otherwise sound -- top view is exactly symmetric about x=50, side profile is coherent nose-left, and internal spec self-consistency (AR 4.09, area 0.198, Re ~170k, CL 0.60, wing loading 48 g/dm2) all checks out.

[snapfit_structure] PRINTABILITY/WEIGHT: 0.95 kg AUW is tight but not fantasy. Honest bookkeeping (3 motors ~90g, ESCs ~40g, 3 servos ~30g, props ~15g, wiring ~30g, 6mm carbon spar ~35g, LiPo 200g, FC/GPS ~30g) leaves ~480g for the printed LW-PLA/PETG shell, which is achievable at 0.9 m span. Kept as-is but the tri-tilt now needs a third tilt servo, eating a little margin.

[blown_wing] REYNOLDS OVERCLAIM (verdict flipped scales -> partially-scales): The concept's own cited evidence undercuts its verdict. The largest quoted benefit — UIUC/Selig CLmax gains up to ~57% — occurs at Re 30,000-80,000 precisely because the turbulent slipstream suppresses the laminar-separation bubble. That bubble-suppression bonus IS a low-Re artifact: at the clean-wing cruise Re of ~200,000 the bubble is already weak, so that mechanism does not transfer to cruise. What DOES survive is the pure dynamic-pressure (powered-lift) q-boost, which is Reynolds-agnostic and helps in the slow transition corridor (~50k-120k). Net: partially-scales, not scales.

[blown_wing] STATIC MARGIN NUMBER CONTRADICTS THE DIAGRAM: The wing chord in the diagram's box units is ~7 (leading edge y=40 to trailing edge y=47). A CG-to-AC gap of (42-38)=4 box units is ~57% MAC of static margin, NOT the claimed +8%. That is a wildly over-stable, near-untrimmable craft as drawn. To actually achieve ~+8% MAC the gap must be ~0.5-0.6 box units, i.e. CG at y~41.3 with AC at y~41.9. The prose and the cg_point coordinate were incompatible; cg_point corrected to y=41.3.

[blown_wing] HOVER THRUST CENTROID AFT OF CG: Motors were placed at y=33,33,55,55 giving a rotor-thrust centroid at y=44, which is ~6 box units BEHIND the (original) CG at y=38. A quad hovers cleanly only when the thrust centroid sits on the CG; as drawn it develops a persistent nose-down pitch in hover that must be fought with differential thrust, wasting control authority. Fixed by moving the CG to y=41.3 (near mid) AND re-spacing the front rotors to y=36 and rear to ~47 so the thrust centroid straddles and coincides with the CG.

[blown_wing] CRUISE-DRAG EFFICIENCY CLAIM HAS THE WRONG SIGN: The claimed '5-8% cruise-drag reduction from the smaller wing' fails a drag audit. Shrinking area ~24% AND dropping aspect ratio 9->6 raises induced drag at cruise CL~0.38 enough that total wing drag goes from ~0.687 N (AR9 unblown baseline) to ~0.723 N (AR6 blown) — the small low-AR wing is actually slightly DRAGGIER in cruise, not less draggy. The parasite saving is real but is more than offset by the induced-drag penalty of low AR. Corrected to claim the honest, defensible gains: reduced wing mass/structure, stiffer easier-to-print wing, and lower transition power — with cruise drag roughly a wash (0 to +/-a couple percent), not a 5-8% win.

[blown_wing] BLOWING FRAMED AS A CRUISE LEVER WHEN IT IS A TRANSITION TOOL: Cruise CL is only ~0.38, far below stall, so essentially no blowing is needed in cruise. The blown-wing q-boost only matters in the slow hover-to-cruise transition corridor. Efficiency prose corrected to state this explicitly rather than implying a cruise-efficiency benefit from blowing.

[blown_wing] AUW IS OPTIMISTIC / BOOKKEEPING DOES NOT CLOSE: The listed components sum to 1.31 kg (0.35 battery + 0.36 motors/props + 0.25 wing/spar + 0.20 fuselage + 0.15 avionics/payload) which already exceeds the stated 1.30 kg AUW, leaving NEGATIVE mass for four servos, tilt gearboxes, yokes, wiring, connectors, and fasteners. Independent wing buildup gives ~270 g vs the claimed 250 g. Realistic AUW is ~1.45-1.5 kg once tilt hardware and wiring are counted. AUW corrected to ~1.45 kg and wing loading/CL/Re recomputed (loading ~85 N/m^2, cruise CL ~0.43 at 18 m/s — still safely sub-stall).

missing.name: Adjustable trailing-edge trim tabs / bendable control surfaces (the 'bend the flaps up' lesson) — decoupling built-in geometry from in-field pitch trim
missing.why: The single most universal thing everyone does with a paper airplane is bend the back edge of the wing up or down to trim it — turning a nose-diving or stalling glider into a stable one without changing the airframe. None of the ten concepts embody field-adjustable/deformable trim: the powered craft rely on gyro/servo authority and the passive gliders (Polyhedra P1, and the glide modes of Albatross/Suzanne) bake pitch trim into fixed printed geometry. A 3D-printed drone concept built around compliant/bendable printed trailing edges or discrete trim tabs (leveraging TPU living hinges already used in Nakamura Locke) directly teaches that small trailing-edge deflection sets equilibrium AoA — the core paper-plane trimming principle — and de-risks the print-once-fly-once problem where a mis-estimated CG makes a fixed-geometry glider unflyable.

missing.name: Wing camber and leading-edge shaping / airfoil from a flat plate (folded-nose leading edge, cambered wing) — the transition from zero-thickness plate to a real lifting section
missing.why: Paper airplanes teach a subtle but foundational aerodynamic lesson: a flat sheet flies poorly, but adding camber (the classic curved-wing 'glider' fold) or a thick folded leading edge dramatically improves lift and stall behavior at low Reynolds number. The entire concept set treats wings as planform/aspect-ratio problems (high-AR booms, box wings, plank) and as thrust-vectoring problems, but none is organized around exploiting the airfoil section itself — precisely the degree of freedom 3D printing unlocks that folded paper cannot (true 3D cambered/reflexed sections, tubercles, wing washout printed directly in). A concept centered on a printed cambered/reflexed airfoil (reflex being what actually makes a tailless plank like Polyhedra P1 trim without a tail) rounds out 'shape of the lifting surface,' which is currently a blind spot.

missing.name: Flat-spin / deep-stall recovery and spin-resistant planform geometry (the 'nose-heavy plane that pancakes vs. the one that spins in') — graceful failure and stall departure behavior
missing.why: A recurring paper-flight lesson is departure behavior at the edge of the envelope: too little nose weight and the plane stalls, pitches up, and falls into a flat spin; the right CG and wing sweep/washout give a gentle mushing descent instead. The concept set covers controlled slow flight (DEP-1 blown-wing transition corridor) and intentional autorotation (Samara, Suzanne feathering), but no concept is designed around passive spin resistance / benign stall departure — geometric washout, wingtip stall delay, or CG-band sizing so the craft mushes rather than tumbles when it runs out of speed or loses power. This is the highest-consequence failure mode for the tailless/flying-wing and quadplane-in-transition designs here, and it is exactly the safety-through-geometry principle paper flight demonstrates most viscerally.
